titolo: How Knight Capital Lost $440 Million in 45 Minutes

shots.voce: Four hundred forty million dollars. Gone in forty-five minutes.
shots.didascalia: Lost in under one trading morning

shots.voce: One company. One morning. And a question nobody could answer: what was the machine doing?
It was August first, twenty twelve.
shots.sotto: Regular trading opens at nine thirty

shots.voce: Knight Capital was a major market maker, based in Jersey City.
Its job: handle huge volumes of stock orders for other firms.
That day, the New York Stock Exchange launched a new program for retail orders. Knight rushed new software to take part.
But one of eight servers never received the update. It still held old, retired code.
When the market opened, that old code began sending orders. Millions of them.
The firm bought high and sold low, again and again, across about one hundred forty stocks.
In about forty-five minutes, it traded over four million shares it never meant to trade.
shots.didascalia: From the opening bell to the shutdown

shots.voce: Knight's own stock collapsed, falling more than sixty percent in two days.
The loss was larger than the firm's entire cash reserves.
Investors stepped in with a rescue, and within months Knight was acquired.
So what was the machine doing? Running code nobody remembered to remove.
